analysis.one_liner: Bans airlines from paying employees incentives for charging passengers add-on fees and from discriminatory pricing.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee with no cosponsors and never got a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The End Airline Extortion Act would make it illegal for airlines to pay employees or contractors bonuses for getting passengers to pay extra fees for things like bags and seat selection as a condition of boarding. It would also bar airlines from charging different fares or add-on fees to passengers based on disability or family status on the same flight. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, especially families and people with disabilities. Anyone who has been pressured at the airport into paying for bags or seat upgrades would face less pressure, because the gate and counter workers imposing those fees could no longer earn incentives tied to how much they collect. Disabled passengers and families would get legal protection against being charged more than other passengers on the same flight for the same service.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits airlines from paying employees or contractors any incentive or fee triggered when a passenger is made to pay a baggage, seating, or other add-on fee as a condition of boarding, removing the direct financial reward for squeezing fees out of travelers at the gate.

Bars airlines from discriminating on the basis of disability status, familial status, or other covered characteristics when setting fares or ancillary fees for the same service on the same flight — for example, charging a disabled passenger or a family with a child more than another passenger for the same seat or bag.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would lose a tool for pushing add-on fee sales through employee incentives, and would face new restrictions on how they price fees for disabled passengers and families.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap or reduce ancillary fees themselves — airlines could still charge the same baggage and seat-selection fees; it only stops employees from being paid incentives tied to imposing them.

The anti-discrimination provision is broad and somewhat vague: it bars charging different fares or fees to passengers with a 'covered characteristic' on the same flight, and carriers and regulators would have to work out how that applies to ordinary differential pricing, which could invite confusion or disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real consumer cost — junk fees for bags and seat selection that airlines tack on — and the ban on paying gate and counter workers commissions for squeezing fees from passengers is a sensible rule that would remove the incentive to badger travelers at the airport. Its strongest part is the discrimination ban, which would protect disabled passengers and families from being charged more for the same service. Drawbacks: it does not cap or even require upfront disclosure of the fees themselves, so airlines could keep charging them freely — they would just lose a small commission mechanic; and the anti-discrimination language is broad enough to invite disputes over what counts as pricing passengers fairly. On balance, a modest but genuine pro-consumer measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2024, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never advanced further before the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hawley introduced the bill on December 10, 2024, less than a month before the 118th Congress ended.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the standard first step — and no further action was ever taken.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines keep charging junk fees and incentive structures untouched.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never considered or reported it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a cosponsor from either party, so no pattern of support or opposition was ever recorded.

industries.note: Carriers would lose the ability to pay front-line workers per-imposed junk fees and could no longer price-discriminate against disabled or family travelers on the same flight. The fees themselves, however, could still be charged.
